newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Baghdad says US, boosting forces, plans new attack.
newsitem.headline: Baghdad says US, boosting forces, plans new attack.

text.p: As America ordered extra troops to Kuwait, a top Iraqi official said on Tuesday that the United States was beefing up its military presence in the Gulf in order to launch another military strike.

Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz made the statement in Baghdad as U.S. President Bill Clinton ordered 3,500 additional ground troops to Kuwait in his confrontation with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

"American pretexts and excuses for the massing of troops and weapons in the Arab Gulf region are aimed at the staging of an aggression on Iraq," Aziz said in a statement carried by the official Iraqi News Agency (INA).
"The preparation for the staging of one aggression after another comes when the Americans find that circumstances are suitable and serve their policies and election interests."
INA said Aziz had sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
A Pentagon official said the U.S. troops would go "in the coming days" and Clinton said they were part of a plan to "keep Saddam Hussein in a box".
They will join 1,500 U.S. soldiers already in Kuwait, a major oil exporter which was overrun by Iraqi troops in a 1990 invasion that triggered the 1991 Gulf War.
Kuwaiti envoys are seeking Arab support for the U.S. buildup and U.S. Secretary of Defence William Perry has consulted often-sceptical allies in the Middle East and Europe.
Perry said on Tuesday that he had found the Western-Arab Gulf coalition "alive and well".
Britain told Kuwait on Tuesday it would despatch troops once more to the Gulf Arab state if necessary to deter Iraq.
The United States said on Tuesday it has sent a fresh message to Iraq telling it not to interfere with Western patrols of no-fly zones in Iraq from which Iraqi aircraft are banned.

The confrontation between Iraq and the United States began late last month when Baghdad's forces intervened to help a Kurdish faction in northern Iraq -- an area closed to them since the end of the Gulf war in 1991.

Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani, whose forces took control of north Iraq last week with backing from Baghdad, plans to tell the United States he is not interested in further deals with Saddam Hussein, a spokesman for his Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) said on Tuesday.
London-based spokesman Dilshad Miran said that Barzani would also ask that the U.S.-led allied air operation to protect northern Iraq from Baghdad's troops be continued.
The State Department said that on Thursday Barzani will meet Robert Pelletreau, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States also wanted to arrange negotiations between Barzani and Jalal Talabani, whose Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) was routed from its northern Iraq strongholds by KDP forces.

Clinton, who faces a presidential election in less than two months, was attacked on Tuesday by opposition Republicans for the lack of impact from two U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq he ordered in reprisal.
"Saddam Hussein is far better off than he was two weeks ago," said Republican Senator John McCain.
Baghdad sought last week to avert another U.S. assault by suspending further missiles attacks on U.S., French and British warplanes patrolling the no-fly zones.

As the U.S. military buildup continued, the U.S. nuclear-powered submarine Pittsburgh passed through the Suez Canal on Tuesday to join a naval force in the Gulf that will include two aircraft carriers. Patriot anti-missile missiles arrived in Saudi Arabia.

Kuwait, the only Arab country to solidly support the current U.S. action, sent envoys around the Middle East on Tuesday to try to persuade Arab governments that the buildup was necessary to deter Iraqi agression.
Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah said after seeing Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak that Kuwait felt threatened.
